claim: Adaptation is driven by the selection for beneficial mutations that provide a fitness advantage in the specific environment in which a population is evolving.
source: Adaptation is driven by the selection for beneficial mutations that provide a fitness advantage in the specific environment in which a population is evolving.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in evolutionary biology, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: Most adaptive evolved lineages show fitness effects in non-home environments.
source: We find that pleiotropy is common, with most adaptive evolved lineages showing fitness effects in non-home environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from bulk fitness assays measuring fitness effects across multiple environments.

claim: Pleiotropic effects of adaptive mutations are unpredictable, being beneficial in some environments and deleterious in others.
source: Consistent with other studies, we find that these pleiotropic effects are unpredictable: they are beneficial in some environments and deleterious in others.
evidence: This claim is supported by both citation to other studies and by data from the current study's fitness measurements.

claim: Lineages with adaptive mutations in the same genes tend to show similar pleiotropic effects.
source: However, we do find that lineages with adaptive mutations in the same genes tend to show similar pleiotropic effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing fitness profiles of lineages with mutations in the same genes.

claim: Ploidy influences the observed adaptive mutational spectra in a condition-specific fashion.
source: We also find that ploidy influences the observed adaptive mutational spectra in a condition-specific fashion.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data showing different mutational spectra in haploid versus diploid populations.

claim: In some conditions, haploids and diploids are selected with adaptive mutations in identical genes, while in others they accumulate mutations in almost completely disjoint sets of genes.
source: In some conditions, haploids and diploids are selected with adaptive mutations in identical genes, while in others they accumulate mutations in almost completely disjoint sets of genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data and mutational spectrum analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: Ecotypes of a species seemed best adapted to their native environment.
source: The idea of a genotype resulting in different fitnesses in different environments has its roots in early botany experiments, first carried out a century ago by Turesson, 1922, who noted that ecotypes of a species seemed best adapted to their native environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Turesson, 1922.

claim: Plants that are adapted to a particular environment were more fit in that environment than those adapted elsewhere, and vice versa.
source: This concept was later extended by Clausen et al., 1948, whose now classic reciprocal transplant experiments showed that plants that are adapted to a particular environment were more fit in that environment than those adapted elsewhere, and vice versa.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Clausen et al., 1948.

claim: Many gene deletions show pleiotropic effects and are often beneficial in some environments yet deleterious in others.
source: These studies revealed that many gene deletions show pleiotropic effects and are often beneficial in some environments yet deleterious in others.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies using the yeast gene deletion collection (Steinmetz et al., 2002; Deutschbauer et al., 2005; Hillenmeyer et al., 2008; Giaever and Nislow, 2014).

claim: E. coli evolved for 20,000 generations often lost various catabolic functions.
source: Early work (Cooper and Lenski, 2000) showed that Escherichia coli evolved for 20,000 generations often lost various catabolic functions, though it was unclear whether such loss was due to pleiotropy of adaptive mutations, or instead was the result of additional non-adaptive mutations due to mutation accumulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cooper and Lenski, 2000.

claim: E. coli evolved at 20°C often, but not always, showed reduced fitness at 37°C.
source: Subsequent work (Bennett and Lenski, 2007) demonstrated that E. coli evolved at 20°C often, but not always, showed reduced fitness at 37°C, suggesting that the adaptive mutations resulted in trade-offs, yet confoundingly that such trade-offs did not always manifest.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bennett and Lenski, 2007.

claim: Trade-offs have been demonstrated between different phases of the yeast growth cycle.
source: More recently, using pooled fitness measurement with barcoded lineages, trade-offs have been demonstrated even between different phases of the yeast growth cycle (Li et al., 2018), likely in large part due to the existence of Pareto optimality fronts (which prevent performance in two traits to be maximized simultaneously) constraining performance between different pairs of growth cycle traits (Li et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Li et al., 2019.

claim: Adaptive mutants selected in one environment frequently showed trade-offs in other environments.
source: A detailed analysis of barcoded yeast adaptive mutants, selected for improved fitness in glucose limited medium, showed that adaptive mutants selected in one environment frequently showed trade-offs in other environments, suggesting that pleiotropy may be global (Kinsler et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kinsler et al., 2020.

claim: When haploid populations were independently evolved in many different environments, the fitness consequences in environments in which they were not evolved were largely unpredictable.
source: The first showed that when haploid populations were independently evolved in many different environments, the fitness consequences in environments in which they were not evolved were largely unpredictable – that is, whether a population evolved specialists or a generalist phenotype was largely due to chance (Jerison et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jerison et al., 2020.

claim: Replicate populations evolving independently displayed very similar pleiotropic profiles within the first few hundred generations, but variability in pleiotropic effects tended to increase among populations over evolutionary time.
source: The second (Bakerlee et al., 2021) showed that replicate populations evolving independently displayed very similar pleiotropic profiles within the first few hundred generations, but that variability in pleiotropic effects tended to increase among populations over evolutionary time with the extent of that variability depending on the evolution environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bakerlee et al., 2021.

claim: Barcoded haploid and diploid yeast populations were evolved in 12 different environments each for up to 440 generations.
source: Barcoded haploid and diploid yeast populations were evolved in 12 different environments (Table 1) each for up to 440 generations.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design and methods used in the study.

claim: In both the diploid and haploid populations evolved in the clotrimazole environment, rapid adaptation was observed, with adaptive lineages largely taking over the population within the first 16–24 generations.
source: In both the diploid and haploid populations evolved in the clotrimazole environment, we observed rapid adaptation, with adaptive lineages largely taking over the population within the first 16–24 generations.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the fluconazole evolution, both the diploid and haploid populations showed rapid adaptation, though the most abundant lineages that took over the population did so more slowly than in the clotrimazole evolutions.
source: Similarly, in the fluconazole evolution (fluconazole), both the diploid and haploid populations showed rapid adaptation, though the most abundant lineages that took over the population did so more slowly than in the clotrimazole evolutions, suggesting that at these drug concentrations the selective pressure is stronger in clotrimazole.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracking data and includes an inference about selective pressure.

claim: The diploid population evolved in glycerol/ethanol evolved more slowly than those in the presence of azole drugs, with the most abundant lineage only exceeding 1% frequency by generation 160.
source: By contrast, the diploid population evolved in glycerol/ethanol evolved more slowly than those in the presence of azole drugs, with the most abundant lineage only exceeding 1% frequency by generation 160.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: In the haploid population evolved in glycerol/ethanol, a single lineage grew to ~50% of the population by generation 150.
source: Finally, in the haploid population evolved in glycerol/ethanol, we observed a single lineage grow to ~50% of the population by generation 150, though several lineages exceeded 1% in frequency.
evidence: This claim is supported by lineage tracking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Adaptation to glycerol/ethanol is a relatively weak selection compared to evolution in the presence of an antifungal drug.
source: Similar to the diploid population evolving in glycerol/ethanol, these data suggest that adaptation to glycerol/ethanol (2% glycerol + 2% ethanol) is a relatively weak selection compared to evolution in the presence of an antifungal drug.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lineage tracking data comparing adaptation rates.

claim: A total of 160 unique mutations in 25 different genes were identified.
source: We identified a total of 160 unique mutations in 25 different genes; most of them were single nucleotide polymorphisms leading to a missense or nonsense mutation (Table 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data summarized in Table 2.

claim: Most of the identified mutations were single nucleotide polymorphisms leading to a missense or nonsense mutation.
source: We identified a total of 160 unique mutations in 25 different genes; most of them were single nucleotide polymorphisms leading to a missense or nonsense mutation (Table 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data summarized in Table 2.

claim: In clotrimazole, only two adaptive gene targets were observed: PDR1 and PDR3.
source: For example, in clotrimazole, we observed only two adaptive gene targets, PDR1 and PDR3, both of which acquired numerous missense mutations irrespective of ploidy, suggesting that these mutations are likely hypermorphic and either dominant or co-dominant.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data and mutational spectrum analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: PDR1 and PDR3 acquired numerous missense mutations irrespective of ploidy.
source: For example, in clotrimazole, we observed only two adaptive gene targets, PDR1 and PDR3, both of which acquired numerous missense mutations irrespective of ploidy, suggesting that these mutations are likely hypermorphic and either dominant or co-dominant.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2.

claim: Mutations in PDR1 and PDR3 are likely hypermorphic and either dominant or co-dominant.
source: For example, in clotrimazole, we observed only two adaptive gene targets, PDR1 and PDR3, both of which acquired numerous missense mutations irrespective of ploidy, suggesting that these mutations are likely hypermorphic and either dominant or co-dominant.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the same genes are mutated in both haploids and diploids.

claim: Both PDR1 and PDR3 are known targets for multidrug resistance.
source: Both PDR1 and PDR3 are known targets for multidrug resistance and such resistance is typically acquired by single missense mutations (e.g. Ksiezopolska et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ksiezopolska et al., 2021 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Multidrug resistance is typically acquired by single missense mutations in PDR1 and PDR3.
source: Both PDR1 and PDR3 are known targets for multidrug resistance and such resistance is typically acquired by single missense mutations (e.g. Ksiezopolska et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ksiezopolska et al., 2021.

claim: In fluconazole and glycerol/ethanol conditions, adaptive targets common to both ploidies as well as numerous genes whose mutation was ploidy specific were observed.
source: However, in fluconazole and glycerol/ethanol conditions, we observed adaptive targets common to both ploidies as well as numerous genes whose mutation was ploidy specific.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data and mutational spectrum analysis shown in Figure 3 and Table 2.

claim: In glycerol/ethanol, genes in the Ras/cAMP pathway were targets in both haploids and diploids, such as IRA1 and IRA2.
source: For example, in glycerol/ethanol, genes in the Ras/cAMP pathway were targets in both haploids and diploids, such as IRA1 and IRA2, which are also known targets of adaptation in glucose limited conditions (Venkataram et al., 2016), where they exert a substantial fraction of their fitness benefit during the respiration phase of the growth cycle (Li et al., 2018);
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: IRA1 and IRA2 are known targets of adaptation in glucose limited conditions.
source: For example, in glycerol/ethanol, genes in the Ras/cAMP pathway were targets in both haploids and diploids, such as IRA1 and IRA2, which are also known targets of adaptation in glucose limited conditions (Venkataram et al., 2016), where they exert a substantial fraction of their fitness benefit during the respiration phase of the growth cycle (Li et al., 2018);
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Venkataram et al., 2016.

claim: IRA1 and IRA2 exert a substantial fraction of their fitness benefit during the respiration phase of the growth cycle.
source: For example, in glycerol/ethanol, genes in the Ras/cAMP pathway were targets in both haploids and diploids, such as IRA1 and IRA2, which are also known targets of adaptation in glucose limited conditions (Venkataram et al., 2016), where they exert a substantial fraction of their fitness benefit during the respiration phase of the growth cycle (Li et al., 2018);
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Li et al., 2018.

claim: Genes involved in heme biosynthesis (HEM2, HEM3) and sensing (HAP1) are adaptive targets only in diploids in glycerol/ethanol.
source: by contrast, genes involved in heme biosynthesis (HEM2, HEM3) and sensing (HAP1) are adaptive targets only in diploids.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Although many gene targets are shared between haploid and diploid populations there are gene targets whose fitness effects differ by ploidy.
source: These patterns reveal that although many gene targets are shared between haploid and diploid populations there are gene targets whose fitness effects differ by ploidy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mutational spectrum data comparing haploid and diploid populations.

claim: Lineages with different barcodes but with identical mutations have similar fitness estimates in each condition.
source: Nonetheless, lineages with different barcodes but with identical mutations have similar fitness estimates in each condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data from bulk fitness assays, as shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: Multiple lineages with distinct barcodes from the glycerol and ethanol condition that carry the same mutation, GPB2-Q602*, have very similar fitnesses across all of the test environments.
source: For example, multiple lineages with distinct barcodes from the glycerol and ethanol condition that carry the same mutation, GPB2-Q602*, have very similar fitnesses across all of the test environments (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Appendix 1—figure 4.

claim: The fitness estimates are reproducible.
source: Thus, the fitness estimates are reproducible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that lineages with identical mutations show similar fitness estimates.

claim: A majority of lineages are not neutral in non-home environments when grown in the BFA.
source: We find that a majority of lineages are not neutral in non-home environments when grown in the BFA, suggesting that pleiotropy is common.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data from bulk fitness assays shown in Appendix 1—figure 5 and Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: For haploid lineages evolved in glycerol/ethanol, the vast majority of lineages have either a positive or negative fitness in at least one other environment in which their fitness was remeasured.
source: For example, for haploid lineages evolved in glycerol/ethanol, the vast majority of lineages have either a positive or negative fitness in at least one other environment in which their fitness was remeasured (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Some diploid lineages evolved in glycerol/ethanol when remeasured in fluconazole had fitnesses comparable to diploid lineages evolved in fluconazole with the top 10% highest fitnesses in fluconazole.
source: For example, some diploid lineages evolved in glycerol/ethanol when remeasured in fluconazole had fitnesses comparable to diploid lineages evolved in fluconazole with the top 10% highest fitnesses in fluconazole (Appendix 1—figures 7 and 7).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: Haploid and diploid lineages adapted in glycerol/ethanol have a negative fitness in pH 7.3.
source: For example, haploid and diploid lineages adapted in glycerol/ethanol have a negative fitness in pH 7.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data from bulk fitness assays.

claim: The strength of the pleiotropic effects is environment-dependent and adaptive mutations can be beneficial, neutral, or deleterious in non-home environments.
source: The strength of the pleiotropic effects is environment-dependent and adaptive mutations can be beneficial, neutral, or deleterious in non-home environments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fitness measurement data across multiple environments.

claim: All mutations that arose from the same evolution in diploid clotrimazole, regardless of gene, have similar patterns of pleiotropy.
source: For some environments, we observed that all mutations that arose from the same evolution, regardless of gene, have similar patterns of pleiotropy. Such a pattern is observed in the diploid mutant lineages that arose in clotrimazole, which all had strong positive fitness effects in clotrimazole and fluconazole yet were mostly neutral/slightly deleterious in all other environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutations selected for in a given home environment, even in the same gene, do not always have the same pleiotropic profiles.
source: However, we also observe instances in which mutations selected for in a given home environment, even in the same gene, do not have the same pleiotropic profiles.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data showing variation in pleiotropic profiles for mutations in the same gene.

claim: In haploid populations evolved in fluconazole, mutations in CSG2 have similar profiles except when remeasured in 37°C and glycerol/ethanol.
source: For example, in haploid populations evolved in fluconazole, mutations in CSG2 have similar profiles except when remeasured in 37°C and glycerol/ethanol.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CSG2-G258C is deleterious at 37°C, and has neutral fitness in glycerol/ethanol.
source: CSG2-G258C is deleterious at 37°C, and has neutral fitness in glycerol/ethanol, while the other CSG2 mutations, CSG2-E234D and CSG2-S28F, have neutral fitness at 37°C and positive fitness in glycerol/ethanol.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: CSG2-E234D and CSG2-S28F have neutral fitness at 37°C and positive fitness in glycerol/ethanol.
source: CSG2-G258C is deleterious at 37°C, and has neutral fitness in glycerol/ethanol, while the other CSG2 mutations, CSG2-E234D and CSG2-S28F, have neutral fitness at 37°C and positive fitness in glycerol/ethanol.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mutations in the same gene, that arose in the same evolution environment, tend to have more similar pleiotropic effects to one another than to mutations in different genes that also arose in the same environment.
source: Overall, we observe that mutations in the same gene, that arose in the same evolution environment, tend to have more similar pleiotropic effects to one another than to mutations in different genes that also arose in the same environment (Appendix 1—figure 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Appendix 1—figure 8.

claim: Pleiotropic effects are environment dependent – what is adaptive in one environment may be adaptive in some environments but also maladaptive in others.
source: Pleiotropic effects are environment dependent – what is adaptive in one environment may be adaptive in some environments but also maladaptive in others.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fitness measurement data across multiple environments.

claim: Adaptation can be cost-free, at least in the conditions in which fitness was measured.
source: While adaptation can lead to pleiotropic effects that are common, strong, and variable, such adaptation can even be cost-free, at least in the conditions in which we measured fitness.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data showing some mutations have neutral or positive fitness in all measured non-home environments.

claim: Diploid lineages evolved in clotrimazole containing a PDR1 mutation are highly fit (fitness >0.2) in both the home environment and fluconazole, yet have a deleterious fitness (fitness <–0.018) in pH 7.3.
source: We observed that diploid lineages evolved in clotrimazole containing a PDR1 mutation are highly fit (fitness >0.2) in both the home environment and fluconazole, yet have a deleterious fitness (fitness <–0.018) in pH 7.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PDR3 mutant lineages evolved in clotrimazole are highly fit (fitness >0.2) in both the home environment and fluconazole but are less deleterious in pH 7.3 compared to PDR1 mutants.
source: On the other hand, PDR3 mutant lineages evolved in clotrimazole are also highly fit (fitness >0.2) in both the home environment and fluconazole but instead are less deleterious in pH 7.3.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: PDR1-L278V and PDR1-C862Y+ are exceptions to the PDR1 lineages and are more like the PDR3 mutant lineages in their fitnesses.
source: There are two exceptions to the PDR1 lineages, PDR1-L278V and PDR1-C862Y+, both of which are more like the PDR3 mutant lineages in their fitnesses.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Adaptive haploid lineages evolved in clotrimazole all show positive fitness in fluconazole.
source: Adaptive haploid lineages evolved in clotrimazole all show positive fitness in fluconazole, which is a very similar condition to clotrimazole.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Many haploid lineages evolved in clotrimazole with mutations in PDR1 show a trade-off in the pH 7.3 condition.
source: Many of these lineages also have mutations in PDR1 and similarly show a trade-off in the pH 7.3 condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Several haploid lineages with mutations in PDR3 show mild positive fitness in fluconazole yet near neutral fitness in all other environments, suggesting cost-free adaptation.
source: Similar to the diploid evolutions, there are several haploid lineages with mutations in PDR3 that show mild positive fitness in fluconazole yet near neutral fitness in all other environments, suggesting cost-free adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4, with an inference about cost-free adaptation.

claim: Not all lineages with PDR3 mutations have cost-free adaptation.
source: However, not all lineages with PDR3 mutations have such cost-free adaptation.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data showing variation among PDR3 mutant lineages.

claim: Two CSG2 mutations (CSG2-S26F and CSG2-E234D) result in cost-free adaptation in haploid lineages that evolved in fluconazole.
source: Similarly, in the haploid lineages that evolved in fluconazole treatment, two CSG2 mutations result in cost-free adaptation, with both CSG2-S26F and CSG2-E234D either being near neutral or conferring a small benefit in the non-home environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The HAP1-V1471 insertion haploid mutant is fit in its home environment (fluconazole), almost equally as fit in glycerol/ethanol, and has either positive or near neutral fitness in all other environments.
source: Finally, we see a similar pattern with the HAP1-V1471 insertion haploid mutant, which is fit in its home environment (fluconazole), almost equally as fit in glycerol/ethanol, and has either positive or near neutral fitness in all other environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cost-free adaptation across a range of substantially dissimilar environments is possible, at least across the conditions in which fitness was remeasured.
source: These examples reveal that cost-free adaptation across a range of substantially dissimilar environments is possible, at least across the conditions in which we remeasured fitness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fitness measurement data showing some mutations have no fitness costs in measured environments.

claim: It is possible that mutations showing cost-free adaptation result in fitness costs in environments in which fitness was not remeasured.
source: It is of course possible that such mutations result in fitness costs in environments in which we did not remeasure fitness.
evidence: This is a speculative statement acknowledging the limitations of the study.

claim: Haploid lineages adapted in glycerol/ethanol with mutations in IRA1 show the same pattern of fitness effects across conditions.
source: For example, haploid lineages adapted in glycerol/ethanol with mutations in IRA1 show the same pattern of fitness effects across conditions (Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: Lineages with mutations in IRA2 show the same pattern of fitness effects as those with mutations in IRA1.
source: Furthermore, lineages with mutations in IRA1's paralog, IRA2, show the same pattern of fitness effects.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: Both IRA1 and IRA2 participate in the Ras pathway.
source: Both IRA1 and IRA2 participate in the Ras pathway suggesting that this pattern may hold true for all genes that participate in this pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of IRA1 and IRA2.

claim: Lineages with mutations in GPB2 have a distinct pattern compared to the lineages with mutations in IRA1 or IRA2.
source: However, we instead see that lineages with mutations in GPB2, another gene in the Ras pathway, have a distinct pattern compared to the lineages with mutations in IRA1 or IRA2, which was also seen in Kinsler et al., 2020.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data and citation to Kinsler et al., 2020.

claim: GPB2 is a gene in the Ras pathway.
source: However, we instead see that lineages with mutations in GPB2, another gene in the Ras pathway, have a distinct pattern compared to the lineages with mutations in IRA1 or IRA2, which was also seen in Kinsler et al., 2020.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of GPB2.

claim: Pleiotropic patterns can be gene specific.
source: This suggests that pleiotropic patterns can be gene specific.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that mutations in different genes in the same pathway show different pleiotropic patterns.

claim: Lineages adapted to the same home environment and with mutations in genes that participate in the same biological pathway (Ras pathway) can have different pleiotropic profiles.
source: Here, we see that even lineages adapted to the same home environment and with mutations in genes that participate in the same biological pathway (Ras pathway) can have different pleiotropic profiles, suggesting that the environment is not the main driving force of pleiotropy, but instead that pleiotropy varies according to target genes and not environment alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fitness measurement data comparing mutations in different genes within the same pathway.

claim: The environment is not the main driving force of pleiotropy, but instead pleiotropy varies according to target genes and not environment alone.
source: Here, we see that even lineages adapted to the same home environment and with mutations in genes that participate in the same biological pathway (Ras pathway) can have different pleiotropic profiles, suggesting that the environment is not the main driving force of pleiotropy, but instead that pleiotropy varies according to target genes and not environment alone.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fitness measurement data.

claim: Ploidy affects the genes in which mutations are selected during evolution.
source: We found that ploidy affects the genes in which mutations are selected during evolution, as seen in the different mutational spectra between haploid and diploid populations evolved in glycerol/ethanol and fluconazole (Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2.

claim: Different trade-offs are observed between haploid and diploid populations evolved in the same environment.
source: We also see different trade-offs between haploid and diploid populations evolved in the same environment.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data comparing haploid and diploid lineages.

claim: In glycerol/ethanol, the haploid adapted lineages have a trade-off at 37°C but the diploid adapted lineages do not.
source: For example, in glycerol/ethanol, the haploid adapted lineages have a trade-off at 37°C but the diploid adapted lineages do not (Appendix 1—figure 5E, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Appendix 1—figure 5E, F.

claim: For clotrimazole treatment, the same genes are targeted in both haploid and diploid populations.
source: However, for clotrimazole treatment, this is not the case: we see the same genes targeted in both haploid and diploid populations evolved in clotrimazole, and we observe that ploidy does not necessarily affect pleiotropy.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: For clotrimazole treatment, ploidy does not necessarily affect pleiotropy.
source: However, for clotrimazole treatment, this is not the case: we see the same genes targeted in both haploid and diploid populations evolved in clotrimazole, and we observe that ploidy does not necessarily affect pleiotropy.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that the same genes are mutated and show similar pleiotropic profiles in both ploidies.

claim: The mutation PDR1-Y864H arose in both haploid and diploid populations evolved in clotrimazole and showed similar pleiotropic profiles in both ploidies.
source: The mutation PDR1-Y864H, which arose in both haploid and diploid populations evolved in clotrimazole, showed similar pleiotropic profiles in both ploidies.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: The haploid and diploid lineages with PDR1-Y864H both show positive fitness in fluconazole and clotrimazole (if fitness is available) and negative or close to zero fitness in all other measured environments.
source: The haploid and diploid lineages with PDR1-Y864H both show positive fitness in fluconazole and clotrimazole (if fitness is available) and negative or close to zero fitness in all other measured environments.
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: The haploid lineage with PDR1-Y864H shows an observably more negative fitness in pH 7.3 compared to the diploid lineage.
source: However, the haploid lineage shows an observably more negative fitness in pH 7.3 (Figure 4, Appendix 1—figure 9).
evidence: This claim is supported by fitness measurement data shown in Figure 4 and Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: HEM2, HEM3, and HAP1 were mutated only in diploid evolutions in glycerol/ethanol and not observed in haploids.
source: We also identified several genes that were mutated only in diploid evolutions, such as those in HEM2, HEM3, and HAP1, which are not observed in haploids evolved in glycerol/ethanol.
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Table 2 and Figure 3.

claim: Mutations in HEM2, HEM3, and HAP1 may be recessively lethal and thus overdominant, such that the heterozygous mutant is more fit than either homozygote.
source: We hypothesize that such mutations may be recessively lethal and thus overdominant, such that the heterozygous mutant is more fit than either homozygote.
evidence: This is a hypothesis or speculation about the nature of these mutations based on their ploidy-specific occurrence.

claim: Prior work suggests that overdominance is a common outcome for adaptive mutations in diploid populations.
source: Although additional experiments will be required to determine how often adaptive mutations arise in diploid populations result in overdominance, prior work suggests that it is a common outcome (Sellis et al., 2011; Sellis et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sellis et al., 2011 and Sellis et al., 2016.

claim: Change in copy number and expression of HXT6/7 is an adaptation observed in glucose limitation that was found to be overdominant.
source: Change in copy number and expression of HXT6/7 is an adaptation observed in glucose limitation that was found to be overdominant.
evidence: This is a statement of prior findings, likely from the cited work of Sellis et al.

claim: Mutants reconstructed to be heterozygous for different combinations of accumulated mutations were found to be overdominant.
source: Other work reconstructed mutants to be heterozygous for different combinations of accumulated mutations and found such mutants to also be overdominant (Aggeli et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aggeli et al., 2022.

claim: Clotrimazole and fluconazole are azoles that target the synthesis of ergosterol, a cholesterol-like component essential to cell membranes in fungi.
source: Both of these antifungal drugs are azoles that target the synthesis of ergosterol, a cholesterol-like component essential to cell membranes in fungi (Cottom and McPhee, 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Cottom and McPhee, 2022 and represents established knowledge.

claim: Despite their similar antifungal mechanisms of action, clotrimazole and fluconazole vary in their strength of selection and adaptive mutational spectra.
source: Despite their similar antifungal mechanisms of action, they vary in their strength of selection and adaptive mutational spectra.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lineage tracking and whole-genome sequencing data comparing the two drug conditions.

claim: The conducted evolutions were short, such that sufficient adaptive mutations were identified in only three of the environments.
source: The conducted evolutions were short, such that sufficient adaptive mutations were identified in only three of the environments (though this reduced the number of neutral hitchhiking mutations and thus it was easier to identify adaptive mutations).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and its limitations.

claim: Short evolutions reduced the number of neutral hitchhiking mutations and thus made it easier to identify adaptive mutations.
source: The conducted evolutions were short, such that sufficient adaptive mutations were identified in only three of the environments (though this reduced the number of neutral hitchhiking mutations and thus it was easier to identify adaptive mutations).
evidence: This is an inference about the benefit of the short evolution time.

claim: Longer evolutions would provide more adaptive mutations in more environments, though disentangling neutral hitchhiking mutations from adaptive driver mutations will be more difficult.
source: Longer evolutions would provide more adaptive mutations in more environments, though disentangling neutral hitchhiking mutations from adaptive driver mutations will be more difficult.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about what would happen with longer evolutions.

claim: Pleiotropy is influenced not only by home environments, but also by several other factors such as ploidy, target genes, and other factors yet to be determined, possibly including strength of selection.
source: Our results suggest that pleiotropy is influenced not only by home environments, but also by several other factors such as ploidy, target genes, and other factors yet to be determined, possibly including strength of selection.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the overall results of the study.

claim: A double barcode system was designed in which one barcode encodes the environment within which a lineage will be evolved and the other is used for lineage tracking within each evolving population.
source: To investigate adaptation and its pleiotropic consequences, we designed a double barcode system (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), in which one barcode is intended to encode the environment within which a lineage will be evolved and the other is used for lineage tracking within each evolving population (as in Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The double barcode approach was devised such that evolved lineages from multiple evolutionary conditions could be pooled and their barcodes used to measure fitness across multiple conditions without concern about DNA barcode sequence collisions.
source: This approach was devised such that we could pool evolved lineages from multiple evolutionary conditions, and use their barcodes to measure fitness across multiple conditions and not be concerned about DNA barcode sequence collisions between adaptive clones isolated from different evolution conditions.
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for the experimental design.

claim: Double barcoded populations of both haploid and diploid S. cerevisiae were generated with sufficient barcode complexity to track hundreds of thousands of lineages evolving in each condition.
source: We generated double barcoded populations of both haploid and diploid S. cerevisiae such that we had sufficient barcode complexity to track hundreds of thousands of lineages evolving in each condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design and methods.

claim: Both haploid and diploid barcoded yeast populations were evolved in 12 conditions in duplicate.
source: We evolved both haploid and diploid barcoded yeast populations in 12 conditions in duplicate.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The evolution environments were chosen with the goal of spanning a wide variety of conditions that had varying timescales of adaptation, different environmental or chemical perturbations, or alternative carbon sources.
source: We chose the evolution environments with the goal of spanning a wide variety of conditions that had varying timescales of adaptation, different environmental or chemical perturbations, or alternative carbon sources (see Methods, Table 1 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a description of the rationale for selecting the evolution conditions.

claim: For each evolution condition, the frequency of barcodes was tracked by amplicon sequencing every 8–24 generations.
source: For each evolution condition ('home' environment), we tracked the frequency of barcodes by amplicon sequencing for one or both of the replicates every 8–24 generations, allowing us to observe the extent of adaptation and to estimate which lineages were likely to contain beneficial mutations.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Barcoded lineages were isolated from a timepoint at which there was substantial adaptation, and whole-genome sequenced to identify mutations that arose during evolution.
source: From each evolution condition, we isolated barcoded lineages from a timepoint at which we determined, if possible, that there was substantial adaptation (see Methods; Supplementary file 2) and whole-genome sequenced lineages to identify the mutations that arose during the evolution.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: A bulk fitness assay (BFA) was conducted in which isolated lineages were pooled into three different pools and their fitness was measured in up to 10 of the original evolution conditions.
source: We then conducted a bulk fitness assay (BFA) in which we pooled the isolated lineages into three different pools and measured their fitness in up to 10 of the original evolution conditions (Levy et al., 2015), capturing their fitness effects in their evolution ('home') environment, as well as the pleiotropic consequences of those mutations in other 'non-home' environments (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods shown in Figure 1.

claim: ~100–750 unique lineages were isolated from each evolution condition.
source: We isolated ~100–750 unique lineages from each evolution condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental data.

claim: The focus was on adaptive clones isolated from three conditions from which more than 30 lineages with identifiable mutations from both haploid and diploid evolutions were isolated.
source: Based on barcode lineage tracking data (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1), we decided to focus on adaptive clones isolated from three of the conditions, from each of which we were able to isolate more than 30 lineages with identifiable mutations from both haploid and diploid evolutions (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis approach based on lineage tracking data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The three focal conditions were: treatment with clotrimazole (2 mg/L), treatment with fluconazole (4 mg/L), and growth in glycerol and ethanol (2% glycerol plus 2% ethanol).
source: These conditions were: treatment with the antifungal drug clotrimazole (2 mg/L), treatment with the antifungal drug fluconazole (4 mg/L), and growth in non-fermentable carbon sources: glycerol and ethanol (2% glycerol plus 2% ethanol).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental conditions.

claim: The types of mutational changes that occurred in diploids or haploids evolved in the same condition appeared similar.
source: While many of these lineages had multiple mutations, we identified presumptive adaptive targets (see Methods) and in so doing, determined the adaptive mutational spectrum for each of the haploid and diploid populations in the three focal evolution conditions: clotrimazole, fluconazole, glycerol/ethanol. We identified a total of 160 unique mutations in 25 different genes; most of them were single nucleotide polymorphisms leading to a missense or nonsense mutation (Table 2; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by whole-genome sequencing data shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: The fitnesses were estimated using the frequency trajectories of each barcoded lineage.
source: The fitnesses were estimated using the frequency trajectories of each barcoded lineage (Methods, Appendix 1—figure 2) and fitnesses for each replicate of a pool correlate well with one another (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Fitnesses for each replicate of a pool correlate well with one another.
source: The fitnesses were estimated using the frequency trajectories of each barcoded lineage (Methods, Appendix 1—figure 2) and fitnesses for each replicate of a pool correlate well with one another (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: Lineages adapted to clotrimazole rapidly took over the BFA populations grown in clotrimazole such that it was not possible to obtain a reliable fitness estimate for lineages in the BFAs grown in clotrimazole.
source: The lineages adapted to clotrimazole rapidly took over the BFA populations grown in the clotrimazole containing fitness remeasurement experiment such that it was not possible to obtain a reliable fitness estimate for lineages in the BFAs grown in clotrimazole.
evidence: This is a description of a limitation in the fitness measurement data.
